ethiopia.title: Ethiopia as a Focal Point Between the Quad and Quintet Coalition on Sudan - horn review
ethiopia.summary:
Ethiopia has emerged as a crucial mediator in the ongoing conflict in Sudan, particularly as tensions escalate between the Quad (the United States, United Kingdom, Japan, and India) and the Quintet (which includes the African Union, the Arab League, the United Nations, and the European Union). The Ethiopian government is leveraging its geographical and political position to facilitate dialogue and peace efforts among the conflicting parties. As violence continues to disrupt Sudan, Ethiopia's role is increasingly recognized as vital for regional stability. The Quad and Quintet coalitions are seeking to coordinate their approaches to address the humanitarian crisis and support peace initiatives. Ethiopia's involvement is seen as essential in bridging the gap between international interests and local realities, aiming to foster a collaborative environment for conflict resolution. The situation remains fluid, with Ethiopia's diplomatic efforts being closely monitored by both coalitions as they strive for a sustainable solution to the turmoil in Sudan.

Password recovery Recover your password your email A password will be e-mailed to you. borkena Ethiopian News and Opinion Home Featured Latest News Business Opinion Video Amharic Entertainment Restaurant Travel Sport Books Blog Business Listings Jobs Support Us Contact Sign in / Join Monday, November 16, 2026 Facebook Linkedin Telegram TikTok WhatsApp Instagram X Youtube Home Ethiopian News Escalating Political Conflicts and Multi-Front Instability Deepen Crisis Across Ethiopia Ethiopian News November 16, 2026 Updated: November 16, 2026 Escalating Political Conflicts and Multi-Front Instability Deepen Crisis Across Ethiopia November 16, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Linkedin Telegram Viber Escalating multi-front violence across Amhara, Tigray, Oromia, and bordering regions leaves over 1,500 dead in two months and triggers major displacement File Photo ( Credit : Crisis Group) By Staff Writer (Nairobi, Kenya) — A sharp resurgence of multi-front armed violence, inter-communal clashes, and military confrontations across multiple regions has pushed Ethiopia into an increasingly volatile security landscape over the past two months, triggering widespread displacement and severe civilian casualties. Data compiled by the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED) indicates that political violence and targeted attacks resulted in 1,556 fatalities across Ethiopia during September and October. This total includes 863 deaths recorded during October alone, with approximately 300 of those victims directly identified as civilians. The vast majority of these incidents were concentrated within the Amhara , Tigray , and Oromia regions, alongside localized escalations in Benishangul-Gumuz , Gambella , South Ethiopia , and the Somali region. Legal and political analysts, speaking to regional media outlets, attribute the persistence and recent spike in coordinated conflicts to a deeply entrenched “conflict-based political economy” and systemic governance gaps. Getachew Gebrekiros Tamre, an expert in law, peacebuilding, and conflict resolution, argued that armed conflict has increasingly been adopted as a functional tool for political enforcement by both state authorities and insurgent factions. “Either the federal government or the regional government uses war as a way of political enforcement, and other opposing forces, to the same extent, have entered into the idea that there is no problem we can solve by sitting down and discussing, so our rights and interests must be enforced through war,” Getachew noted, emphasizing that structural drivers continue to perpetuate cyclical instability. A primary catalyst for the recent regional escalation has been the renewal of military hostilities between federal forces and Tigray units. Dr. Awol Kassim Allo, a law lecturer at the University of Sheffield and an East African political analyst, suggested that the resumption of conflict in the north, combined with the activities of insurgent coalitions, has strategically overstretched state security forces. He pointed to the emergence of alliances among various armed opposition groups—including a seven-member coalition aiming to establish a transitional government and remove the administration of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed—as a major factor contributing to simultaneous security pressures across multiple fronts. The human cost has been severe across several administrative zones. In the Oromia Region, localized attacks and armed raids in areas such as Arsi (including Shirka and Arsi Robe woredas) and the former Horo Gudru Wollega Zone resulted in over 118 deaths during mid-October clashes. Regional authorities have blamed allied insurgent networks for the violence, reporting the detention of numerous combatants. Meanwhile, the Benishangul-Gumuz region also witnessed lethal violence, with the regional Police Commission confirming that 52 people were killed in an armed assault in the Buldigu woreda of the Assosa Zone. In Moyale town along the southern border, overlapping territorial disputes between Borana-Oromo and Garre-Somali communities erupted into heavy-weapon clashes, driving more than 50,000 refugees across the international border into Kenya and precipitating an urgent humanitarian emergency. Critics and human rights advocates have sharply questioned the state’s capacity to ensure public safety. Dr. Awol told BBC Amharic that the widespread proliferation of violence demonstrates that the government has failed in its primary duty to protect citizens, arguing that officials must acknowledge systemic security shortcomings. While the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission (EHRC) stated that it is actively investigating violations across affected regions—including recent fact-finding missions in Central Ethiopia, Horo Gudru, East Wollega, and Arsi—Commission officials noted that while certain types of localized assaults remain frequent, overall recording trends reflect ongoing, systemic security challenges rather than an entirely unprecedented scale of operation. As regional administrations and federal security forces grapple with concurrent insurgencies, humanitarian actors warn that without renewed political dialogue and comprehensive security reforms, civilian populations across the country will continue to bear the heaviest toll of the deepening instability. __ Join our Telegram Channel : t.me/borkena Like borkena on Facebook Join the conversation. ethiopia.title: News - Federal High Court Rejects Media Authority's Jurisdictional Objection, Decrees Hearing of Addis Standard's Case
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: News - Federal High Court Rejects Media Authority's Jurisdictional Objection, Decrees Hearing of Addis Standard's Case - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: News - Federal High Court Rejects Media Authority's Jurisdictional Objection, Decrees Hearing of Addis Standard's Case 16 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — The Federal High Court has declined the Ethiopian Media Authority's preliminary objections challenging its jurisdiction to hear a lawsuit filed by JAKENN Publishing PLC over the revocation of Addis Standard's online media registration certificate, clearing the way for the substantive case to proceed. In a ruling delivered by the Lideta Division's First Administrative Direct Suit Review Bench on Thursday 12 November, the court held that the Authority is an administrative institution subject to judicial review under the Federal Administrative Procedure Proclamation No. 1183/2020, notwithstanding its independent institutional status and accountability to the House of Peoples' Representatives. The court dismissed the Authority's argument that its regulatory decisions should be exclusively governed by the Media Proclamation No. 1238/2021 and its amendment, Proclamation No. 1374/2025, rather than the administrative procedure law. Addressing the Authority's contention that it was an independent democratic institution outside the scope of the administrative procedure legislation, the court pointed out that Article 4(1) of the Media Proclamation, which establishes the Authority as a federal government office with legal personality. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines It further ruled that the fact that the Authority is accountable to parliament rather than the Council of Ministers under Article 4(2) does not exempt it from judicial scrutiny under the administrative procedure framework. "The fact that the respondent institution is accountable to the House of Peoples' Representatives rather than the Council of Ministers ... does not provide a legal basis to claim that it is an independent institution that should be exempted from review," the court ruled. The court also rejected the Authority's argument that the subsequent enactment of the amended Media Proclamation had replaced the administrative procedure framework. It observed that Article 2(11) of the amended media law expressly allows parties aggrieved by decisions of the Authority's Management Board to petition the Federal High Court within 30 working days. According to the court, this provision does not establish a separate procedural system that excludes the application of the administrative procedure Proclamation. "The subsequent enactment of Proclamation No. 1374/2025 did not alter or establish a separate procedural system distinct from the Administrative Procedure Proclamation," the ruling stated. The court further addressed the Authority's failure to respond to JAKENN's administrative grievance challenging the certificate revocation, finding that the alleged failure to issue a decision within the prescribed period constitutes a matter that can be examined under Article 33 of Proclamation No. 1183/2020. Under Article 33(1) and (2), administrative institutions are required to issue decisions without undue delay, and failure to issue a decision within the appropriate timeframe is deemed a rejection of the request. The court noted that JAKENN had submitted its grievance to the Authority's Management Board on February 26, 2026, challenging the revocation of Addis Standard's registration certificate , but the Board had failed to issue a decision within the mandatory 30 working days. Consequently, it concluded that the company's petition followed proper legal requirements to appear before the court as a challenge to an administrative decision allegedly withheld beyond the legally prescribed timeframe. The lawsuit, filed on May 7, 2026, challenges the Authority's February 25, 2026 announcement revoking Addis Standard's online media registration certificate. JAKENN argued that the decision was made without prior written or verbal warning, without specifying the reports allegedly in violation of media ethics, Ethiopian laws and national and public interests, and without giving the organization an opportunity to respond to the allegations. The company also submitted to the court that it had submitted complaints to the Authority's Management Board on February 26 and March 6, followed by a supplementary complaint through its lawyers on April 27, but received no decision. JAKENN requested the court to overturn the revocation , reinstate the registration certificate and protect its media freedom so that it could resume operations. The Authority maintained that its regulatory functions were governed by the special media legislation and that the court lacked jurisdiction to entertain the case under the Federal Administrative Procedure Proclamation. The court, however, ruled that the Authority's routine regulatory functions, including registering online media and issuing, renewing, suspending and revoking registration certificates, fall within its administrative activities and are subject to the applicable administrative review framework. The court scheduled a hearing for December 9, 2026, to address the substantive issues of the case, which includes allegations that the revocation was made without proper warning or opportunity for response. This ruling marks a significant development in the ongoing regulatory dispute between the media outlet and the Authority.

ethiopia.title: Ethiopia's Second Tigray War - Same Battlefield, Different Political Reality
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia's Second Tigray War - Same Battlefield, Different Political Reality - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia's Second Tigray War - Same Battlefield, Different Political Reality 16 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — In November 2020, federal forces entered Mekelle, and Addis Abeba declared the war in Tigray finished. Seven months later, Tigrayan fighters walked back into the city, and within a year they were pushing towards the capital. In October 2026, federal troops and their Tigrayan allies took Mekelle again . The government now speaks of restoring order and installing a new regional administration. The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) says it will keep fighting from the mountains. Ethiopia has seen this film before. The question is whether its leaders believe the second round will end differently. The evidence of the past six weeks suggests it will not, and for reasons that go deeper than battlefield tactics. The political landscape that made the 2020 campaign possible has collapsed. The war being fought today is a war over sovereignty: who holds power in the Ethiopian state and on whose terms. No capture of a regional capital has ever settled that question. The argument is simple. A government can hold a city and still lose the country. Ethiopia's federal leadership is treating the recapture of territory as proof that the state's authority has been restored. In practice, each town held without political consent becomes another garrison to supply, another road to defend, and another grievance to inherit. The coalition of 2020 no longer exists Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The first Tigray war was winnable in the short term because Tigray stood almost alone. The TPLF had run the Ethiopian state for close to three decades, and its fall from power in 2018 left a long list of people who wanted it weakened. Eritrea wanted to settle an old score. Amhara forces wanted security and the return of land they regarded as theirs, above all Western Tigray. Afar authorities mobilized to repel Tigrayan incursions. Federal leaders wanted to end a rival center of power. These actors shared little except an enemy, but that was enough to surround Tigray, cut its services, and starve its supply lines. That alignment has dissolved. After the Pretoria agreement of November 2022, the federal government moved in 2023 to disband regional special forces, and the Amhara Fano militias turned their guns on Addis Abeba. Three years later, Fano commanders sit in the same coalition as the TPLF they once fought. The founding statement of the Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival was read on Tigray Television in September 2026 by Zemene Kassie, chairman of the Amhara Fano National Movement. A scene like that was unthinkable in 2021. The Tigrayan camp has also split, and that cuts the other way. Getachew Reda, who once spoke for the TPLF at Pretoria, is now an adviser to Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed . Government-aligned Tigrayan fighters, under the Tigray Peace Force (TPF) banner, entered Mekelle alongside federal troops. Addis Abeba has learned to fight Tigray partly with Tigrayans. That is a real advantage, but it is a borrowed one. A coalition built on the defection of individual leaders is far thinner than one built on the shared fears of entire regions. Assab and the new regional map Nothing has rearranged the Horn of Africa faster than Addis Abeba's demand for the sea. Since 2023, the prime minister has repeated that landlocked Ethiopia must secure direct access to the Red Sea. Senior officials, including the air force commander in October 2026 , have named the Eritrean port of Assab as the goal. Asmara reads these statements as a declared intention to seize its territory, and it has said so formally in notes to the UN Security Council . The consequences were predictable. In 2020, Eritrean troops fought beside federal forces in Tigray. In October 2026, witnesses reported Eritrean soldiers crossing into northern Ethiopia near Zalambessa , and Ethiopia responded with drone strikes on Eritrean vehicles near Adigrat . Each government now accuses the other of starting a war. Addis Abeba alleges that Asmara funds and arms the opposition. Eritrea denies backing the TPLF , but its strategic logic is plain: an Ethiopian army tied down at home is an army that cannot march on Assab. In early October, Ethiopia expelled Eritrean diplomats , closed its embassy in Asmara, and declared 10 Eritrean diplomats persona non grata, prompting Eritrea to sever diplomatic ties . The move follows overnight explosions in Addis Abeba amid renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia. The breakdown in relations raises the risk of miscalculation and further escalation as formal diplomatic channels close. The regional balance has shifted with it. In early October, Egypt, Somalia, Eritrea, and Sudan met and declared that only states with a Red Sea coastline should govern the waterway, a position widely read as a message to Ethiopia. Sudan's civil war adds another layer, with fighters, weapons, and sponsors moving across a porous border in both directions. Ethiopia's neighbors no longer need to love its rebels to help them . They only need to fear its government more. This is the most important difference between 2020 and 2026. The first war was a domestic confrontation with a foreign ally on the government's side. The second is a domestic confrontation embedded in an interstate rivalry, and the government's own rhetoric helped build it. Towns are not command structures The federal military still holds clear advantages. It commands the air, it has more drones, and it has recovered Mekelle, the Afar towns lost in September, and much of Tigray's urban belt. None of that should be dismissed. But capturing a city is the easiest phase of a counterinsurgency, and the hardest phases follow. The Tigray Defense Forces withdrew from Mekelle rather than fight for it street by street. Their leadership survived, and by mid-October they had launched a counteroffensive against federal supply lines in central Tigray . Federal units then pulled back from several localities on the Eritrean border to reinforce the interior, and Tigrayan forces reportedly moved into at least one of the towns they vacated. This is the pattern of 2021 in miniature: an army that wins the cities, then discovers that the countryside decides how long it can keep them. The arithmetic gets harder when the other fronts are counted. Federal forces are already fighting Fano in Amhara and the Oromo Liberation Army in Oromia . Every brigade sent to guard a Tigrayan highway is a brigade withdrawn from somewhere else. A government can advance on several maps at once while slowly running out of the soldiers, fuel, and money needed to hold any of them. If Tigrayan forces keep their command intact and keep cutting roads, Addis Abeba will face a choice it cannot win cheaply: pour more troops into Tigray or contain the advances in Amhara and on the approaches to the capital. A coalition built on the defection of individual leaders is far thinner than one built on the shared fears of entire regions." None of this makes a rebel victory inevitable. The Alliance for Survival has no named joint commander; its members are separated by hundreds of kilometers, and several of them are militarily weak. A cascade of federal reversals is a possible scenario, not a forecast. The point is narrower. The government's current gains do not amount to the end of the war, and treating them as if they did repeats the error of November 2020. Whose state? Beneath the military campaign lies an older belief: that whoever controls the center must keep it at any cost, because losing power means losing safety. Ethiopia's modern history gives that belief some grounding. The imperial order and the Derg both fell to armed rebellion, and the collapse of the TPLF-led coalition was followed by war within two years. Each change of regime brought reprisals against the communities associated with the old one. That history now shapes how parts of the political class defend the present government. For some Oromo elites, an administration led by an Oromo prime minister has become a guarantee of their community's place in the state, even when its conduct contradicts the democratic demands that brought it to power in 2018. In this view, sharing power looks like surrender, and criticism looks like an attack on the community itself. The flaw in this reasoning is that a leader's ethnicity does not make the state belong to the people who share it. Oromia itself is a battlefield. The Oromo Liberation Army has fought federal forces there since 2018, and it now sits in the Alliance for Survival on the argument that the government betrayed Oromo self-determination. Ordinary Oromo farmers face drone strikes, forced recruitment, and disrupted markets like everyone else. Binding a community's future to one government's survival leaves that community exposed when the government falls, and it pushes neighbouring communities to see it as an obstacle rather than a partner. The same trap exists on every side. Tigrayan, Amhara, and Somali politicians have each, at different moments, told their people that only control of a particular government could keep them safe. Ethiopia will not find stability until no community needs to own the state in order to survive inside it. What the opposition owes Ethiopians Criticism of the government does not amount to an endorsement of its armed opponents. The Alliance for Survival unites groups that killed each other's fighters and displaced each other's civilians only a few years ago. Its members have agreed on one goal, the removal of the Prosperity Party government and a transitional administration, and they have set aside almost everything else. Alliance representatives have said openly that territorial disputes have been tabled until after victory . That is the coalition's weakest point. Western Tigray is claimed by both Tigrayan and Amhara leaders. Afar and Somali and Oromo communities contest land along their shared boundary. Wartime atrocities committed by federal, TPLF, Fano, and Eritrean forces have never been accounted for. A coalition that cannot say how it will settle these questions is asking Ethiopians to trade one war for the promise of another. The alliance's founding proclamation commits members to resolving disputes through dialogue. Its credibility will rest on whether it publishes concrete terms on territory, civilian protection, and accountability before it asks anyone to fight for it. About three-quarters of a million people were still displaced inside Tigray before the September fighting began. Recruitment drives empty villages, military spending crowds out schools and clinics, and inflation erodes household budgets across the country. A prolonged war consumes the money Ethiopia would need for recovery while producing the grievances that feed the next rebellion. Ethiopia's partners can help by changing what they count. The African Union, the United States, the Gulf states, and the European Union have tended to follow the war through maps, which town fell this week and which road reopened. A better yardstick is civilian safety, humanitarian access, and whether any party is offering credible political terms. Pressure on Addis Abeba and Asmara to step back from the Assab confrontation matters just as much, because a war between the two states would draw in Egypt, Sudan, and the Gulf and shut the door on any internal settlement. The way out is not mysterious. It requires an inclusive national dialogue that the armed opposition can actually join, a renegotiated political settlement that protects the rights of Ethiopia's nations and nationalities while keeping the state intact, and a security arrangement in which losing an election does not mean losing protection. None of that is easy. All of it is easier than a third capture of Mekelle. In 2020, Ethiopia's leaders believed that taking a city would close a political question. Six years later, the city has changed hands again, and the question is larger than ever. Holding Mekelle is within the government's reach. Holding the country requires something the army cannot deliver: the consent of the people who live in it. AS Editor's Note : Muktar Ismail Issack is a regional analyst and a former UN staff member. The Ethiopian government’s focus on territorial control does not address deeper issues of sovereignty and political legitimacy. The current war is intertwined with regional rivalries, particularly with Eritrea, which has escalated tensions. While federal forces maintain military advantages, the challenges of sustaining control over captured territories and managing multiple fronts are significant. The ongoing conflict risks further destabilization, as historical grievances and ethnic divisions continue to shape Ethiopia's political landscape. The need for a comprehensive dialogue on governance and accountability remains critical for lasting peace.

ethiopia.title: Ugandan Traditional Leaders Champion Local Talent At All Africa Leather Fair in Addis Ababa
ethiopia.content: Africa: Ugandan Traditional Leaders Champion Local Talent At All Africa Leather Fair in Addis Ababa - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Africa: Ugandan Traditional Leaders Champion Local Talent At All Africa Leather Fair in Addis Ababa 16 November 2026 The Independent (Kampala) Addis — A delegation of Ugandan traditional leaders has called for stronger collaboration between cultural institutions and diplomats to promote Uganda's heritage and drive continental growth, during a courtesy visit to the Embassy of the Republic of Uganda in Addis Ababa. The leaders, in Ethiopia for the 6th Continental African Traditional Leaders Conference (Africa Celebrates 2026), met with embassy officials on Friday to discuss how Uganda's cultural institutions can work closer with diplomats to share the country's rich heritage, keep communities united, and stimulate real growth across Africa. The delegation included Emorimor Papa Paul Sande Emolot of Teso, Juliet Among Emolot Atomeileng, Queen of Teso, Isabaruuli Isabarongo Mwatyansozi Mwogezi Butamanya, Cultural Leader of Buruuli, and Sir Jude Mike Mudoma, the Omukuuka of Bamasaba. Later, the leaders visited the Addis International Convention Center for the 15th All African Leather Fair (AALF 2026) and the All Africa Leather Awards, where they congratulated Ugandan designer Yoram Atuhamize of Jora Shoes Co. (U) Ltd, who was named one of the Top 15 African Leather Exhibitors and Designers. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Atuhamize caught the judges' attention with his socially conscious footwear under the "Ride to Live Africa Safety Initiative." The Royals praised his creativity and hard work, noting that seeing Ugandan craftsmanship shine on a continental stage is a proud moment for the entire country. The 6th Continental African Traditional Leaders Conference, running from November 10-15 at the African Union Headquarters, brings together kings, queens, and cultural elders from over 46 African nations and the diaspora. Delegates signed the historic Addis Ababa Declaration, launching the African Traditional Leaders Council (ATLC) to enable monarchs and chiefs to work alongside national governments on shared goals. The conference also highlighted the role of traditional leaders in resolving local disputes, preserving African languages and values, and connecting cultural leaders with initiatives like the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) to champion homegrown businesses and create opportunities for youth. ethiopia.title: Tigrayan Youths Face Mounting Execution Fears in Saudi Arabia - Caretaker Admin Pleads With Fed. Govt to Intervene
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Tigrayan Youths Face Mounting Execution Fears in Saudi Arabia - Caretaker Admin Pleads With Fed. Govt to Intervene - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Tigrayan Youths Face Mounting Execution Fears in Saudi Arabia - Caretaker Admin Pleads With Fed. Govt to Intervene 16 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Hundreds of Ethiopian migrants, many of them young people from Tigray who fled conflict and economic hardship in search of work, remain at risk of execution in Saudi Arabia, as mounting executions over drug-related offences intensify concerns about fair-trial violations and the Ethiopian government's response. Haish Subagadis, head of the Tigray Caretaker Administration Youth Bureau Head, says families are increasingly desperate as reports of executions continue to emerge and fears grow over the fate of detainees held in Saudi Arabia's southern regions. In an interview with Addis Standard , Haish said information obtained through the Ethiopian community in Saudi Arabia indicated that approximately 520 Ethiopians across the country had been sentenced to death, with Tigrayans constituting the majority. He said around 200 were detained in the Khamis Mushait, south-west Saudi Arabia, and Abha, the capital city of Aseer Province near the Red Sea in southwest Saudi Arabia, where families are particularly concerned about a new wave of executions. "Now, around 31 have been executed; in this past week alone, seven were executed," he said, adding that approximately 169 remained in the group he was discussing. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Haish said the transfer of approximately 50 detainees from Khamis Mushait to Abha in the days preceding the interview had heightened fears among their families that executions could be imminent . He said parents were struggling to obtain information and repeatedly appealing for intervention. "Be a voice for our children; they went there in search of work and should not die in that country. This is inhumane," he quoted the families as saying. The figures provided by the regional caretaken administration official could not independently be verified by Addis Standard . However, his account comes amid growing documentation by international rights organizations of Ethiopian nationals being executed in Saudi Arabia for drug-related offences, despite international calls to abolish capital punishment for crimes that do not involve intentional killing. A migration crisis rooted in conflict and exploitation The accounts point to a migration crisis in which the consequences of Ethiopia's conflict, economic pressures and inadequate protection for migrant workers are converging with Saudi Arabia's increasingly punitive anti-drug campaign. Haish said many of the young people now facing capital punishment left Tigray following the 2020-2022 war, which displaced communities, disrupted livelihoods and left many young people without viable economic opportunities. Some travelled through Yemen to reach Saudi Arabia, often relying on informal brokers and intermediaries to arrange their journeys and employment. He alleged that some were deceived or pressured into transporting packages across the border without knowing their contents. According to him, brokers would instruct them to carry items along their journey, exposing them to drug-trafficking charges when they entered Saudi Arabia. Because these youths have never left the country before, do not know the laws of the land, do not understand the language, and lack legal knowledge, they do not know what they are facing Haish Subagadis He also raised concerns that young people travelling in groups could face collective punishment when one member was found carrying prohibited substances. Addis Standard could not independently establish the circumstances of individual arrests or convictions. The regional official said the detainees' vulnerability was compounded by their unfamiliarity with Saudi Arabia's legal system, language barriers and limited access to legal representation. He alleged that some were convicted without having Arabic-language court documents translated or receiving adequate legal advice. "Because these youths have never left the country before, do not know the laws of the land, do not understand the language, and lack legal knowledge, they do not know what they are facing," Haish said. He argued that defendants who cannot understand the charges against them or communicate effectively in court are deprived of a meaningful opportunity to defend themselves. His account echoes concerns raised by international rights organizations about the treatment of foreign nationals facing capital punishment in Saudi Arabia. Human Rights Watch (HRW), in a July 2026 report, said Saudi authorities had executed at least 17 Ethiopian nationals since the beginning of the year for drug-related offences, including five men executed on July 27. The organization said at least 79 other Ethiopians remained at imminent risk of execution on similar charges. HRW also documented cases in which court hearings lasted only minutes, without lawyers or interpreters, leaving defendants unable to understand or challenge the charges against them. The African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights subsequently expressed concern over reports that Ethiopian migrants facing execution may have been denied adequate legal representation, interpretation services and consular assistance. In a July 22 statement, it urged Ethiopia to pursue diplomatic and legal avenues to secure reviews of the convictions and strengthen protection for its nationals abroad. Executions rise as Saudi Arabia intensifies its anti-drug campaign The scale of the executions has become increasingly difficult to separate from Saudi Arabia's intensified campaign against drug trafficking . Haimanot Ashenafi, Amnesty International's regional researcher for the Horn of Africa, told Addis Standard that the number of Ethiopian nationals sentenced to death and executed in Saudi Arabia had risen sharply in recent years, particularly following the kingdom's declaration of a "war on drugs." "Ten years ago, three Ethiopians were executed in Saudi Arabia in one year, whereas in the first eight months of 2026 alone, 20 Ethiopians were executed for drug-related offenses, and we know that more people have been executed since then," she said. Amnesty's records, she added, showed that at least 36 Ethiopian nationals were executed for drug-related offences in 2025. The figures illustrate the increasing exposure of Ethiopian migrants to capital punishment for offences that do not involve intentional killing. Amnesty's broader documentation shows that Saudi Arabia carried out a record 356 executions in 2025, including 240 for drug-related offences. Foreign nationals accounted for 78% of those drug-related executions. There is a clear pattern showing that this campaign disproportionately impacts marginalized communities, including migrant workers Haimanot Ashenafi Haimanot said the kingdom's "zero tolerance" approach to drug-related offences had contributed directly to the increase, with migrant workers and other marginalized communities disproportionately affected. "There is a clear pattern showing that this campaign disproportionately impacts marginalized communities, including migrant workers," she said. Amnesty has repeatedly called on Saudi authorities to abolish the death penalty, including for drug-related crimes. The organization maintains that capital punishment should not be imposed for offences that do not involve intentional killing, consistent with international human rights standards. The vulnerability of Ethiopian nationals is also documented in Amnesty's research into the experiences of foreign defendants. Its investigations have identified serious disadvantages confronting migrant workers as they navigate recruitment systems, detention and the Saudi judicial process, including inadequate legal representation and interpretation. The pattern raises questions beyond the individual convictions: whether vulnerable migrants recruited through informal networks have the means to understand the risks of their journeys, access protection when detained and defend themselves against potentially irreversible sentences. Diplomatic response under growing scrutiny Beyond the circumstances of the convictions, both interviews raise questions about the adequacy of Ethiopia's diplomatic response and the extent to which its nationals are receiving protection while facing capital punishment abroad. Haish said the Tigray Interim Administration had previously approached the Ethiopian Consulate in Saudi Arabia through written appeals and in-person representations involving relatives of the detainees. However, he said these efforts had yet to produce a resolution. "We assume that perhaps the effort on the part of the Ethiopian government is insufficient, as there has been no resolution to date," he said. He urged Addis Abeba to intensify diplomatic engagement with Riyadh, arguing that Ethiopia's relations with Saudi Arabia should provide an avenue for negotiations aimed at commuting the sentences and securing the release of the detainees. "Diplomatic efforts must be stepped up; young people at a tender age who went to a foreign country in search of work should not be sentenced to death over matters they know nothing about," he said. Amnesty International has also pressed the federal government to take a more sustained diplomatic approach. Haimanot said the organization had engaged Ethiopian federal officials in recent months, calling for increased support for migrants on death row, particularly through stronger consular assistance. "The federal government must engage in sustained, high-level diplomatic efforts with Saudi authorities on behalf of Ethiopian nationals currently sentenced to death," she said. The calls come amid broader efforts by Ethiopia to repatriate undocumented nationals detained in Saudi Arabia. However, the return of undocumented migrants under mass repatriation and pardon arrangements does not necessarily resolve the cases of those convicted and sentenced to death for drug-related offences. Amnesty has previously warned that releases and repatriations should not obscure the continuing risks faced by Ethiopian nationals on death row. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church's Patriarch has also appealed for intervention to halt the executions , adding religious leadership to mounting calls from families, rights organizations and regional institutions. A crisis extending beyond the death row For Haimanot, the cases cannot be understood solely as a question of criminal justice. They are also a reflection of the circumstances driving Ethiopians into dangerous migration routes in the first place. "These migrants travel through one of the world's most dangerous migration routes," she said. "We must also recognize that many are driven to take this path by the current realities in Ethiopia, where the wider population faces multiple, overlapping crises exacerbated by conflict, economic hardship, and social challenges." The observation places the plight of the detainees within a wider pattern of displacement, irregular migration and labor vulnerability. For many young people from conflict-affected Tigray, migration was not simply an economic choice but an attempt to escape the consequences of war and the absence of sustainable livelihoods. Yet the journey through Yemen, where migrants face exploitation by smugglers and brokers , can expose them to further dangers before they even reach their intended destination. Once detained in Saudi Arabia, language barriers, limited access to lawyers and inadequate consular assistance can leave them particularly vulnerable to criminal proceedings carrying irreversible consequences. The immediate concern remains the fate of those already sentenced to death. Haish said families in Tigray were living with the uncertainty of not knowing whether their children would be among those executed next, particularly following the reported transfer of detainees between facilities. "Listening every week to news that 'this many have been executed' is extremely heavy and difficult for morale," he said, appealing to international media, human rights advocates and diplomatic actors to help prevent further executions. He called for clemency and the release of the detainees, arguing that young people who travelled abroad seeking employment should not lose their lives without having had a meaningful opportunity to defend themselves. ethiopia.title: Tribute - Veteran Ethiopian Leftist Leader and Me'isone Co-Founder Dr. Negede Gobeze Dies At 83
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Tribute - Veteran Ethiopian Leftist Leader and Me'isone Co-Founder Dr. Negede Gobeze Dies At 83 - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Tribute - Veteran Ethiopian Leftist Leader and Me'isone Co-Founder Dr. Negede Gobeze Dies At 83 16 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Dr. Negede Gobeze, a veteran Ethiopian political figure, legal scholar and co-founder of the All-Ethiopia Socialist Movement (Me'isone), died in Brussels on November 13, 2026, at the age of 83. Born in Dessie in October 1943, Negede studied economics at Addis Abeba University College before pursuing further studies in France, where he earned a Ph.D. in law from Aix-Marseille University. He emerged as a prominent figure in Ethiopia's student movement during the 1960s, serving as president of the Ethiopian Students' Union in France and later the Ethiopian Students' Union in Europe. In 1968, he co-founded Me'isone, alongside other leftist intellectuals, including Haile Fida. Following the 1974 student revolution, Me'isone initially aligned itself with the Derg military government. Negede served in the Provisional Office for Mass Organizational Affairs (POMOA) between 1975 and 1977. He later broke with the military government and went into exile in Europe. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines During his years in exile, he remained active in Ethiopian political opposition and advocacy, founding several organizations, including COSETH in 1980 and GRAPECA in 1990. He also helped establish independent media initiatives, including Radio Selam and Keste Damena, and later co-founded the European-based Ethiopian discussion forum Deldeye. Beyond political organizing, Negede was a prolific writer whose work explored Ethiopian politics, constitutional reform and history. His publications included the Amharic book Yidres le Ginbot ke Yekatit , examining the trajectory of the revolutionary movement of the 1970s. He also wrote poetry. His political legacy remains contested. While supporters remember him as a committed revolutionary intellectual who advocated democratic reform and contributed to Ethiopia's political discourse, critics have questioned Me'isone's role and responsibility during its alliance with the Derg, a period marked by widespread repression and political violence. His death marks the passing of a figure whose political life and writings were closely intertwined with some of the most consequential and contested chapters of modern Ethiopian history. Sudan’s military says Ethiopia has allowed Sudanese paramilitary forces battling the army to use its territory to set up camps, launch drones and stage cross-border attacks. In early November, the Sudanese military filed complaints against Ethiopia with the U.N. Security Council and the African Union’s Peace and Security Council, saying it submitted evidence to back up its case. Within days, Ethiopia expelled six staff members of a Sudanese Consulate and ordered the mission closed. Ethiopia says the Sudanese military supports rebels fighting Ethiopian federal forces in its Tigray border region, where fighting returned in September, shattering a 2022 peace agreement. Each country denies the other’s accusations, and The Associated Press could not independently verify their claims. But the tensions — compounded by competing regional alliances and contentious issues over resources and disputed territory — risk a wider regional conflict. Jervin Naidoo, a senior political economist at Oxford Economics Africa, told the AP that the situation “raises the risk that instability inside Ethiopia becomes another front in Sudan’s war — and vice versa.” Here’s a closer look at what’s behind the escalation and how it could impact the wider region: Sudan’s military says Ethiopia backs Sudanese paramilitary forces Sudan was plunged into war in April 2023, when long-simmering tensions between the army and paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, or RSF, turned into all-out fighting. So far, at least 59,000 people have been killed, according to Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, or ACLED, a conflict monitor, though aid groups warn that the real number is likely much higher. Some 13 million people have been displaced. The war, now in its fourth year, has left the Sudanese military in control of the north, east and central regions, including Sudan’s Red Sea ports and its oil refineries and pipelines. The RSF and its allies control western Darfur and parts of Kordofan along the border with South Sudan — both regions rich in oil fields and gold mines. The latest flashpoint in the war is in Sudan’s Blue Nile province, which borders Ethiopia. In late August, the Humanitarian Research Lab, a Yale University research group that uses satellite imagery to monitor conflicts, found an increase in military vehicles and equipment at an Ethiopian military base in Asosa, a city near the Sudanese border. Based on satellite imagery, the Yale group confirmed the buildup was linked to the RSF. “The RSF is engaged out of Ethiopia … to try to open a second front,” said Nathaniel Raymond, head of the research group. Ethiopia says Sudan’s military backs the Tigray rebels Fighting resumed in September in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region, where the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, or TPLF, and Ethiopian federal troops fought between 2020 and 2022, when a peace deal was signed. Later that month, Ethiopia’s army chief, Field Marshal Birhanu Jula, suggested that Sudan, Eritrea and Egypt were supporting rebel troops who at the time had captured several strategic towns. The allegations drew sharp denials from the three neighbors. In early November, Ethiopia expelled the six staff members of Sudan’s mission in Asosa and closed the consulate. Naidoo, from Oxford Economics Africa, warned that continued fighting in Tigray could divert Ethiopia’s attention from its myriad other issues and increase the risk of weapons and fighters flowing across the border with Sudan. “All the ingredients are present for an intensifying proxy war between Ethiopia and Sudan that further destabilizes both countries,” said Alan Boswell, Horn of Africa project director at the International Crisis Group. Unresolved disputes, competing political alliances and a flashpoint border Relations between Sudan and Ethiopia have deteriorated since late last year, when the RSF established camps on Ethiopian territory, according to Ladd Serwat, senior Africa analyst at ACLED. In October, a drone strike blamed on the RSF hit a gathering of displaced people on Sudan’s border with Ethiopia and killed 41, said the Emergency Lawyers rights group, which tracks the war in Sudan. “Sudan and Ethiopia don’t operate in a vacuum; their relations amid these current domestic conflicts are shaped by external backers,” said Serwat, adding that Ethiopia is allied with the United Arab Emirates while Sudan is part of an Egypt-Eritrea regional alliance. Turkey has been balancing, backing both Khartoum and Addis Ababa, he said. Serwat added that Ethiopia’s support for the RSF is primarily logistical, while the UAE remains its main backer, funding camps and supplying weapons. The UAE has repeatedly denied any involvement in Sudan’s war. Other issues have also marred relations, including Ethiopia’s construction of a huge dam — Africa’s largest dam — on the Blue Nile, the main Nile River tributary. The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam near the Ethiopia-Sudan border cost about $5 billion and was completed in 2025, aiming to boost Ethiopia’s power production and economy. But it has triggered a dispute with Egypt and Sudan, which have called for a legally binding agreement on the dam’s filling and operation to protect their own water resources. Another issue is the disputed border region of Al-Fashaga, where Ethiopian farmers have long cultivated the area’s fertile soil, according to the International Crisis Group. In late 2020, Sudanese troops moved in to reassert control over the area as Ethiopian troops were distracted fighting with the Tigray rebels. The Sudan-Ethiopia tensions may not have gained much attention, but if ignored, they could escalate further and lead to mass displacements of people, Raymond’s Yale group said. ___ Associated Press writer Khaled Kazziha in Nairobi, Kenya, contributed to this report. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs gave the advice in a statement issued yesterday by its spokesman, Mr Oluwafemi Adeniyi, in Abuja. Adeniyi said Addis Ababa, located about 2,355 metres (7,726 feet) above sea level, had lower atmospheric pressure and reduced oxygen availability, which could pose health risks to some travellers. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines He disclosed that Nigeria's Diplomatic Mission in Addis Ababa recorded 16 deaths, involving Nigerians transiting through the city in 2026, reportedly linked to health complications associated with high altitude. According to him, although healthy individuals can adapt to reduced oxygen levels, people with certain pre-existing medical conditions, especially cardiovascular and respiratory diseases, may face increased health risks. He urged Nigerians whose medical conditions could be aggravated by high altitude to exercise caution and seek appropriate medical guidance before embarking on journeys involving transit through the city. The spokesman stressed that the advisory was not intended to discourage Nigerians from travelling to or transiting through Addis Ababa. Rather, he said, it was aimed at ensuring that medically vulnerable travellers were adequately informed of the potential risks and took necessary precautions. "Government places a high premium on the health, safety and wellbeing of Nigerians, therefore urge travellers to make informed decisions and take appropriate precautions where existing medical conditions may increase their vulnerability during travels," he said. Adeniyi reaffirmed the ministry's commitment to providing timely information and guidance to Nigerians travelling abroad to safeguard their welfare and safety. Read the original article on This Day . ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Leads a Week of Green Diplomacy As Red Sea Access Push Gains International Momentum
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Leads a Week of Green Diplomacy As Red Sea Access Push Gains International Momentum - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia Leads a Week of Green Diplomacy As Red Sea Access Push Gains International Momentum 15 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) The second week of November 2026 marked a significant period in Ethiopia's diplomatic engagement, as the country stepped up its global climate leadership at COP31 in Türkiye while its longstanding aspiration for sovereign access to the Red Sea gained further international attention. From advancing climate finance and green development partnerships to strengthening Africa's voice in global climate negotiations, Ethiopia used the COP31 platform to reinforce its diplomatic standing ahead of hosting COP32 in Addis Ababa in November 2027. At the same time, growing international recognition of Ethiopia's strategic interests in Red Sea access, alongside renewed discussions over the equitable utilization of the Nile waters, brought the country's development priorities into sharper regional and international focus. Together, these developments underscored Ethiopia's increasingly assertive diplomatic engagement, anchored in its pursuit of sustainable development, regional cooperation and a greater role in shaping issues of strategic importance to Africa and the wider world. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Ethiopia Takes Center Stage in Global Climate Diplomacy Ethiopia emerged as a prominent diplomatic voice at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), held in Antalya, Türkiye, where leaders and delegations from nearly 200 countries gathered to address the mounting challenges of global climate change. As the incoming host of COP32, Ethiopia used the international platform not only to showcase its homegrown climate initiatives but also to advocate for stronger international cooperation, accessible climate finance and practical solutions that address the needs of vulnerable communities. Addressing the COP31 Leaders' Summit, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed called for predictable, timely and affordable climate finance, emphasizing that international climate commitments must translate into tangible support before disasters strike. The Premier stressed that climate action is not simply an environmental undertaking for Ethiopia but a fundamental pillar of its economic policy and national development strategy. "In Ethiopia, climate action is economic policy," he said, highlighting the devastating effects of recurring El Niño-related droughts and floods on agricultural production, livelihoods and community resilience. He noted that climate-related disasters continue to displace families, undermine economic gains and prolong recovery, even after rainfall returns and floodwaters recede. Against this backdrop, the Prime Minister underscored Ethiopia's efforts to strengthen community-level preparedness and equip local governments to anticipate climate risks, protect livelihoods and respond before disasters escalate. He also highlighted the country's broader climate vulnerabilities, noting that more than 90 percent of Ethiopia's electricity is generated from hydropower, making changing rainfall patterns a critical concern for national energy security and electricity supplies to neighboring countries. The effects of rising temperatures and changing rainfall patterns also threaten Ethiopia's forests and agricultural landscapes, including the country's globally renowned Arabica coffee, which remains an important source of livelihoods, export earnings and national identity. Highlighting Ethiopia's homegrown development philosophy of Medemer (Synergy), Abiy explained how the country is mobilizing communities, institutions and resources around shared climate and development objectives. The Green Legacy Initiative, through which millions of Ethiopians participate in large-scale tree-planting campaigns, has seen more than 56 billion seedlings planted to date. The initiative is contributing to land restoration, forest expansion, employment creation and improved livelihoods. The Premier further reaffirmed Ethiopia's commitment to expanding renewable energy, promoting climate-resilient agriculture, protecting urban environments and accelerating electric mobility as part of its broader green development agenda. His message reinforced Ethiopia's position that climate action must go beyond declarations and translate into measurable development outcomes, particularly for countries facing disproportionate climate risks despite contributing relatively little to global emissions. Building the Road to COP32 in Addis Ababa Beyond its high-level political engagements, Ethiopia intensified diplomatic consultations to lay the groundwork for a successful and inclusive COP32. The country's high-level delegation, led by Foreign Minister and COP32 President-Designate Gedion Timothewos and Finance Minister and COP32 Chief Negotiator Fitsum Assefa, held extensive discussions with the COP31 Presidency, negotiating groups, participating countries and international partners. The engagements focused on ensuring a smooth transition from COP31 to COP32, strengthening trust among negotiating parties and building consensus around an implementation-oriented climate conference in Addis Ababa. Ethiopia's approach seeks to position COP32 as a platform that moves beyond climate pledges towards concrete action, with particular emphasis on climate finance, adaptation, resilience and the priorities of developing countries. The opening of the Ethiopian Pavilion at COP31 further strengthened the country's visibility, bringing together diplomats, members of the Ethiopian delegation, partner organizations and international participants to showcase its climate initiatives, investment opportunities and green development experience. The pavilion also provided an important platform for promoting Ethiopia's renewable energy potential, Green Legacy achievements, sustainable agriculture and climate investment opportunities ahead of COP32. Intensive Diplomatic Engagements on the Sidelines of COP31 Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed also used the COP31 gathering to advance Ethiopia's bilateral and multilateral relations through a series of high-level meetings with world leaders. Among his engagements was a meeting with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan in Antalya ahead of the COP31 Leaders' Summit, reflecting the importance Ethiopia attaches to strengthening relations with its strategic partners. The Premier also held discussions with Barbadian Prime Minister Mia Mottley, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Iraqi President Nizar Mohammed Saeed, Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, Qatar's Amir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani and Botswana's President Duma Gideon Boko. The engagements provided opportunities to discuss bilateral cooperation, shared development priorities, climate action and broader regional and international issues. Ethiopia's diplomatic presence at COP31 thus extended beyond climate negotiations, reinforcing its commitment to building strategic partnerships and expanding cooperation across regions. Ethiopia's Red Sea Access Aspiration Gains International Recognition While Ethiopia was advancing its climate diplomacy in Antalya, its pursuit of sovereign access to the Red Sea also attracted renewed international attention, with prominent political figures and foreign defense officials expressing recognition of the country's strategic interests. As Africa's second-most populous nation and one of the region's major economies, Ethiopia has consistently argued that its landlocked status presents significant economic and strategic constraints, particularly given the growing importance of maritime trade to its long-term development. The country has maintained that its aspiration for sea access is rooted in legitimate geographical, historical, economic and strategic considerations, while emphasizing the importance of peaceful engagement, dialogue and mutually beneficial arrangements. Former Prime Minister of Côte d'Ivoire and President of the Ivorian Popular Front, Pascal Affi N'Guessan, recently described Ethiopia's quest for sovereign sea access as a legitimate national aspiration. Speaking to ENA in Addis Ababa, Affi N'Guessan expressed hope that outstanding issues could be resolved through constructive dialogue and compromises acceptable to all parties. "I believe that the ambition of Ethiopia is legitimate, and we hope that these questions will find solutions acceptable to all parties, through good compromises that allow everyone to recognize that this is the path that enables the entire region to move forward," he said. He emphasized that mutual understanding and cooperation were essential to ensuring that competing interests do not become obstacles to regional development and stability. His remarks added to growing international discussions surrounding Ethiopia's maritime aspirations and the broader implications of sea access for economic integration and regional cooperation in the Horn of Africa. Similarly, French and Danish defense attachés recognized Ethiopia's legitimate interest in Red Sea access, highlighting its potential contribution to regional stability, maritime security and efforts to combat terrorism. Speaking to ENA, French Defense Attaché Colonel Damien Cypryk described Ethiopia's aspiration as legitimate, linking maritime access to the country's development and stability. "Access to the Red Sea for Ethiopia is a perfectly legitimate act because it is a question of development and stability," he stated. The defense officials also underscored Ethiopia's importance as a major regional actor, noting that its participation in regional security mechanisms could contribute to safeguarding the strategically important Horn of Africa and its surrounding maritime routes. Their remarks highlighted the broader strategic dimension of Ethiopia's maritime aspirations, which extend beyond trade and economic considerations to encompass regional security, stability and cooperation. Nile Development: Ethiopia Reaffirms Its Position on Equitable Utilization Meanwhile, the equitable utilization of the Abay (Blue Nile) waters remained another important dimension of Ethiopia's regional development diplomacy. Water and Energy Minister Habtamu Itefa urged Egypt to modernize its domestic water management practices, reconsider water-intensive agricultural activities and seek Ethiopia's consent for development projects involving Nile waters. The Minister's remarks reaffirm Ethiopia's position that the Nile should serve as a source of shared prosperity and development rather than a basis for perpetuating historical inequities. Ethiopia has consistently maintained that the equitable and reasonable utilization of transboundary water resources is essential to ensuring the development rights of all riparian countries, while promoting cooperation and avoiding unnecessary regional tensions. The completion of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), achieved despite considerable financial and diplomatic challenges, remains a major expression of the country's determination to harness its natural resources for national development. A Week Reflecting Ethiopia's Expanding Diplomatic Ambitions All in all, Ethiopia's engagements during the second week of November reflected a broader diplomatic strategy that connects climate leadership, economic transformation, regional security and sovereign development interests. At COP31, the country strengthened its international profile as an emerging voice in global climate negotiations, while laying the diplomatic groundwork for COP32 in Addis Ababa. Its extensive bilateral engagements further demonstrated its determination to build partnerships around shared development and global challenges. At the same time, international recognition of Ethiopia's Red Sea access aspirations and renewed discussions over equitable Nile utilization brought its strategic interests into greater international focus. As Ethiopia prepares to host COP32 in 2027, it is increasingly positioning itself not merely as a participant in international discussions but as a country seeking to shape the global development agenda, advance African priorities and promote solutions to some of the most consequential challenges facing the continent and the wider world. The National Intelligence Agency of ‌Somaliland (NIA) said in a post on X late on Sunday that it had been monitoring the US nationals since they arrived and ​conducted a “lengthy investigation” into their activities. NIA Director-General Jama Mohamoud Egal, ​Somaliland’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the US State Department ​did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Somaliland, which declared independence from Somalia in 1991, occupies a strategic location at the juncture of ​the Indian Ocean and Red Sea. Last December, Israel became ​the first country to recognise it as a sovereign state, and its ‌government ⁠has been lobbying for recognition from additional countries, including the United States. According to a person familiar with the matter, the five Americans work for a company called Parallel Black. A ​November 4 ​letter seen by ⁠Reuters shows they were invited by Somaliland’s Foreign Affairs Minister Abdirahman Dahir Adam to conduct ​feasibility studies for potential investments. The person said ​the five ⁠Americans left Somaliland on an Ethiopian Airlines flight on Monday afternoon. Parallel Black, which was registered less than two months ago ⁠in the ​US state of Delaware, did not ​immediately respond to requests for comment. وأوغندا. ونخصص هذا الموضوع للحديث عن القنوات الناقلة لمباراة السودان ضد السنغال اليوم في تصفيات كأس أمم إفريقيا 2027 مع الموعد والتشكيلة، وعن أهم العناوين المرتبطة بها. لمتابعة أحداث مباراة اليوم بين السودان والسنغال لحظة بلحظة اضغط هنا. ويدخل المنتخب السنغالي هذه المباراة من أجل تأكيد علو كعبه على نظيره السوداني بعد الفوز في مباراة الذهاب لحساب الجولة الـ3 بـ4 أهداف مقابل واحد، مواجهة عرفت تألق نجوم السنغال بقيادة هداف نادي أستون فيلا الإنجليزي نيكولاس جاكسون الذي وقع الهدف الأول، في حين تلقى المنتخب السوداني الخسارة الثانية على التوالي وبنفس الحصيلة من الأهداف بعد خسارته من منتخب موزمبيق. المتصدر ووصيفه إلى الحدث الإفريقي الأبرز، ما يفرض على هذا المنتخب الذي يقوده المدرب الغاني كويسي أبيا تحقيق نتائج جيدة في الجولات الـ3 الأخيرة من أجل تعزيز حظوظه في التأهل في المركز الثاني عن هذه الإسماعيلية المصرية (winwin) 14 نوفمبر 2026 خاص | المريخ السوداني يحسم ملفات مهمة قبل الاستئناف المريخ الدوري السوداني الممتاز كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin يواصل فريق المريخ الأول والرديف تحضيراتهما لاستئناف منافسات الدوري الرواندي والنسخة الجديدة من الدوري الممتاز السوداني، وذلك بعد فترة التوقف الدولي التي جاءت في توقيت مناسب، عقب الإقصاء من الدور التمهيدي الثاني لدوري أبطال أفريقيا. ويستعد الفريق الرديف للعودة إلى البلاد للمشاركة في النسخة 31 من الدوري الممتاز، عقب اختتام معسكر ناجح بمدينة الإسماعيلية المصرية، خاض خلاله عددا مقدرا من المباريات التجريبية. روموالد راكوتوندربي يقود المريخ في الممتاز نفى عضو بارز في إدارة نادي المريخ، فضل حجب اسمه، في حديث خاص لموقع "winwin"، كل ما تردد بشأن نية الإدارة إسناد مهمة تدريب الفريق الأول إلى المدرب روموالد راكوتوندربي، والتعاقد مع مدرب محلي لقيادة الفريق الرديف. وأكد المصدر استمرار المدرب الملغاشي في منصبه، وإشرافه على الفريق الرديف في مباريات الدوري الممتاز، مشيرا إلى استمرار جندي نميري في قيادة الفريق الأول بالدوري الرواندي بتكليف من الإدارة. اقرأ أيضًا: مهددًا بالتصعيد لـ"كاس".. المريخ يربك اتحاد الكرة السوداني الهلال يستعيد لقب الدوري ويقصي المريخ من السباق العربي وشدد المتحدث على أن الإدارة حددت أهداف مشاركتها في المسابقة الرواندية، معربا عن ثقته في المدرب المحلي، إلى حين التعاقد مع مدير فني أجنبي، بناء على توصية المدير الرياضي الذي تجري مشاورات حاليا للتعاقد معه. winwin يكشف موعد عودة المريخ إلى السودان وأكد football.summary: يواصل فريق المريخ السوداني، الأول والرديف، استعداداته لاستئناف الدوري الرواندي والدوري الممتاز السوداني بعد فترة التوقف الدولي. جاء ذلك عقب إقصاء الفريق من دوري أبطال أفريقيا. الفريق الرديف أنهى معسكره في الإسماعيلية المصرية، حيث خاض عدة مباريات تجريبية. نفى مصدر في إدارة النادي الشائعات حول تغيير المدرب، مؤكدًا استمرار المدرب الملغاشي روموالد راكوتوندربي في قيادة الفريق الرديف، بينما سيستمر جندي نميري في قيادة الفريق الأول في الدوري الرواندي. الإدارة حددت يوم 20 نوفمبر موعدًا لعودة الفريق الرديف إلى السودان، حيث سيبدأ مشواره في الدوري الممتاز بمواجهة فريق كوبر في 25 من الشهر. كما أكدت الإدارة أنها تتريث في اختيار مدير رياضي ومدرب أجنبي لضمان اتخاذ قرارات مدروسة، مع وضع خطط لضمان ظهور قوي في الدوريين الرواندي والسوداني.
